content.title: General response
content.comment: We would like to thank you all for your valuable feedback and suggestions. As you pointed out, we thought it is necessary to revise the overall structure of the manuscript and the experiment results. Therefore, we have decided to withdraw this Manuscript. Thank you for your feedback, which will help a lot in improving the manuscript in the future.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The main point of the paper is to show that it is possible to extend Fourier Neural Operators with pseudo-differential integral operators instead of Fourier integral operators. The authors then go on to predict the solution of several PDEs (from the heat equation to the Navier Stokes equation, through Darcy flow) through the resulting structure.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: The paper is interesting, especially on the numerical side (see detailed comments below) which seems to indicate an improvement in the  smoothness of the prediction returned by the pseudo differential neural operator (i.e. Neural Operator architecture combined with a pseudo differential integral operator defined on a Neural network encoding the symbol).  I do have some concern with (1) The strength/level of novelty (The notion of pseudo-differential integral operator is not very different from the notion of Fourier integral operator. As an illustration of this, the authors indicate that one of the differences between the Fourier integral operator of Li et al. and the Pseudo differential integral operator introduced in the paper lies in the spatial dependence (i.e. 'x') of the symbol. Yet as shown in the paper, the dependence on x can be moved outside the Fourier integral and therefore only appears as an additional factor.) (2) The organization of the paper. Most of the paper (page 3 for example) is devoted to the introduction of pseudo differential operators and pseudo differential symbols which are well established concepts. Some space could be better used , e.g. to introduce graphical/diagram representations of the Networks and/or additional numerical experiments.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I think the paper should be reorganized in order to more clearly indicate the connection to Fourier integral operators. In particular, I think that the whole first 5 pages could be summarized in one page consisting of (1) introduction of the Notion of Fourier Neural operator 
(2) Explaining that one wants to extend the notion of Neural operator by replacing the Fourier integral operator (required to be bounded and linear) with a pseudo differential operator. (3) Give the main result showing that the pseudo differential operator is indeed bounded
content.summary_of_the_review:
page 3

- Definitions 2.1 and 2.2. can (should?) be removed and replaced by a reference. You could again some space by removing line (8). The space could then used to properly introduced some of the subsequent notations (see my comments below)
- In definition 2.1. What does ‘m’ represent? Does that encode some regularity ?
- connection between Fourier integral operator and Pseudo differential operator? 

page 4
- I don’t understand why parametrizing the symbol with a neural network will necessarily make it smooth. I.e. you could very well have overfitting with a neural network
- In section 3.1. Just above section 3.2. “that connects between the Euclidean symbol and the restricted Euclidean symbol ”  —> “that connects the Euclidean symbol and the restricted Euclidean symbol” or “that bridges the gap between the Euclidean symbol and the restricted Euclidean symbol”
- before Definition 3.1. you should recall the definition of the difference operator \Delta

page 5

- (11) is a discretization of the integral (7). I may be wrong but this does not look to me like the DFT
- if I understand well, a toroidal symbol is a discretization of a Euclidean symbol. Why not add a sentence like this somewhere? I think this would improve readability
- section 3.3 what is the Gaussian Error Linear Unit?
- Equation (13) I think it should be W_2 and Z_2 given your definition of a(x) and a(\xi)
- In (12) and (14), you don’t introduce the notation <\xi>. Do you refer to the average \int_\mathbb{R} \xi d\xi ?
- I don’t see why the fact that the derivatives of all order are bounded and that the derivative of GELU decays rapidly implies (14)
- You use the word “Therefore” before and after (15). I would remove one of them

page 6
- In Theorem 3.6. what do you mean by “extends” to a linear operator ? 
Numerical results (pages 7/8/9)
- I find it surprising that there is such a difference between the results of the Fourier Neural Operator and the Pseudo Differential Operator with the symbol a(\xi) (without spatial dependence). I think this should be better documented
- In the Navier Stokes section, you indicate that you rely on a recurrent architecture. It would be interesting to know how the error propagates in such an architecture. Since you re-use the prediction from time t at time t+1, there must be some accumulation of errors. How are you limited 
- In the Navier Stokes section, I find it surprising that the time dependent model performs consistently more poorly than the PDNO that does not depend on time. Also, you should provide more details on the time dependent model. Does the dependence on time mean that you now include skip connections? How does the complexity of the time dependent model compare with the complexity of the stationary architecture? Can’t we expect a time dependent model to be more appropriate than a stationnary model?
- You indicate that the time dependent model does not use a recursive structure ? What do you mean ?
- We clearly see an improvement in the smoothness of the solution compared to the prediction from Fourier Neural Operators but this improvement is not clearly addressed. Why can one get something smoother and closer to the physics when using PDIO than when using FIO? Why does the prediction from FIO appear more granular?

What matters when training machine learning models is how different the training examples are from the data on which one wants to obtain a prediction. In this case, we don’t really have intuition on this. How are previous time frames (for Navier Stokes for example varying with respect to the frame returned by the model). It would definitely be interesting to know more about this.  

===============================================

Typos

===============================================

- On page 2, first item in your list of contributions : “The symbol of the Fou and pseurier integral operator is only depend on \xi and not depend on position x ” —> “only depends” and “does not depend on ”
- same page, same item, “guaraneteed” —> “guaranteed”
- page 3, below Equation 2, “using the message passing on graph networks” —> “Using message passing”
- page 3, section 2.2. “using the convolution theroem” —> “theorem”
- same page, same section “can be interpreted as the general conecept” —> “can be extended as the extension/generalization” and “concept”
- in section 2.3. “From 1960s, PDOs were derived from differential operators and have been studied” —> “pseudo differential operators have been studied since the 1960’s” ?
- section 2.3. “and the \hat{f}(\xi) .. “ —> “and \hat{f}(\xi)”
- Page 7, below Equation (20) “In the experiment for heat theta_1, \theta_2equation ” —> “for the heat equation”
- same page, below Equation (20) : “approximate time dependent symbol accurately” —> “approximate the time dependent symbol accurately”
- In the section on the Darcy Flow: “We use 1000 train pairs” —> “training pairs” ?

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a pseudo-differential integral operator (PDIO) which generalizes Fourier integral operators, such that the neural version -- the pseudo-differential neural operator (PDNO) -- is a generalization of the Fourier neural operator (FNO). Such pseudo-differential integral operators can be defined as a generalization of differential operators by introducing symbols as functions of the coordinates and the Fourier modes. In PDNO, the symbols are split into a network that takes the coordinates as input and a network that takes the Fourier modes as input. The resulting PDNO are ablated against FNOs on Darcy flow and Navier-Stokes equations.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
-	The comparison of the learned symbol and the analytical symbol on the 1D heat equation is very intuitive and help my understanding.
-	It is shown that the symbol network is contained in a toroidal symbol class, which implies that the PDIO with the symbol network is a continuous operator in the Sobolev space.
-	In general I like the idea that the weights of the Fourier modes are parametrized by an MLP.

Weakness:
-	Table 1 suggests that the baseline models have a lower training but much higher validation error. This clearly suggests overfitting. Which regularization methods have been used on the baseline models? How do the validation curves look like?
-	I expect the proposed PDNO architecture to better model different time horizons, i.e. dependencies on t? Or different grids? Yet in the paper, I only see experiments with fixed gird sizes and time horizons. Would an extension to non-regular output grids be possible? 
-	As shown in Table 5 in the appendix, the proposed method is roughly a factor 5 slower than the FNO baseline, can this be mitigated?
-	Am I right that the symbol networks for each PDNO block get the same inputs, which are the coordinates in the spatial and the Fourier domain. Isn’t that a bit redundant? Maybe I misunderstand, please clarify. 
-	In general, I think it would massively help the paper to compare to the experiments which are introduced in Lu et al. or at least discuss this direction.


Lu, Lu, et al. "A comprehensive and fair comparison of two neural operators (with practical extensions) based on fair data." Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering 393 (2022): 114778.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clear enough written to understand the main ideas and concepts. The idea is novel, however a somehow better experimental evaluation of the benefits of the idea would help.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper introduces PDNO which generalizes Fourier neural operators (FNO). The motivation and theoretical background are easy to follow. At the current stage it is somehow a bit unclear to me how much the proposed PDNO really helps, especially since input grids and time windows are fixed during training. Furthermore, compared to the two baseline methods which show lower losses on the training set, the reported test set losses are lower. I would like to have this outlined in a bit more detail.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presented a new operator network inspired by the pseudo-differential integral operator for learning solution operators of PDEs. The new operator network extended the FNO by adding a symbol function parameterized by a neural network. The effectiveness of the proposed method is verified by Darcy flow and Navier-Stokes problems.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: The paper is well-written and easy to follow. 

Weaknesses: The idea of using pseudo-differential integral operators for building operator networks is very naïve. Similar ideas appeared already in the literature, though being used in different contexts. See the references below. The assumption that the symbol function is separable rules out many nonlinear PDEs. I would expect a nonseparable symbol can potentially improve the performance for some PDEs, especially for nonlinear problems.

Refs:
[1] G Gupta, X Xiao, P Bogdan,  Multiwavelet-based operator learning for differential equations, NeurIPS 2021

[2] J Feliu-Faba, Y Fan, L Ying Meta-learning pseudo-differential operators with deep neural networks, Journal of Computational Physics, 2020
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is easy to read. However, the interest of the proposed method is incremental.
content.summary_of_the_review: I am inclined to reject the paper due to lack of sufficient novelty.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper propose the pseudo-differential integral operator (PDNO), a modification based on FNO to get a smooth and more general operation. The authors mainly use a symbol network to gaurantee the smoothness of the integral operator and provide theoratical proofs on it. PDNO is tested in Darcy flow and Navier stokes equations and outperform two SOTA operators in some of the test.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
Introducing the concept of pseudo-differential operator in neural operator design is interesting and the authors give a sound theoratical discussion on the architecture design for the smoothness gaurantee of the neural operator.  
The performance gain in Darcy flow case is obvious, which to some extent demonstrate the effectiveness of PDNO.

Weakness: 
Although the operator R in the experiment of FNO is independent of the input x or its frequency terms, FNO paper actually discussed the method to parametrizing R with the information of x. The authors may refer to section 4 in FNO paper. This hurts the novalty of this paper.

In addition, FNO paper says that such parametrization does not help the performance, but in your paper, the finding seems opposite, as is shown in the result of PDNO(a(\xi)) table 1. It would be better if the author can discuss more about the difference.

There are some flaws in writing, e.g., 
1. The last sentence in introduction '(Figure 1.' should have a right bracket.
2. Most of the discussion in section 2.4 is dependent on section 3, so I recommend to put it at the end of section 3.
3. In the 2nd sentence of section 4.1, intput -> input.
4. The last sentence of the first paragraph in section 5.3 is unreadable.
5. Some tables are too small, which hurts the readability when printed.

In the case of Navier-stokes equation, PDNO only shows obvious advantages over the other two baselines with viscosity=1e-5, so the performance is not significant enough.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clear for most of the parts, except some obvious flaws in writing. Introducing pseduo-differential operator is noval but not significant enough and the resulting changes in neural operator architecture and the performance improvements are limited.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is clearly writing but the resulting novalty in neural operator design is limited. In addition, the result is not strong enough to demonstrate the advantage.

content.title: Pseudo-Differential Integral Operator for Learning Solution Operators of Partial Differential Equations
content.abstract: Learning mapping between two function spaces has attracted considerable research attention. However, learning the solution operator of partial differential equations (PDEs) remains a challenge in scientific computing. Fourier neural operator (FNO) is recently proposed to learn the solution operators with an excellent performance. In this study, we propose a novel pseudo-differential integral operator (PDIO) to analyze and generalize the Fourier integral operator in FNO. PDIO is inspired by a pseudo-differential operator, which is a generalization of a differential operator and characterized by a certain symbol. We parameterize the symbol by using a neural network and show that the neural-network-based symbol is contained in a smooth symbol class. Subsequently, we prove that the PDIO is a bounded linear operator, and thus is continuous in the Sobolev space. We combine the PDIO with the neural operator to develop a pseudo-differential neural operator (PDNO) to learn the nonlinear solution operator of PDEs. We experimentally validate the effectiveness of the proposed model by using Darcy flow and the Navier-Stokes equation. The results reveal that the proposed PDNO outperforms the existing neural operator approaches in most experiments.
